message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary as a BLACK BOX. The C++ library source is NOT available and you must NOT look for it.

Binary: /workspace/dataset/test20_executable
Invoke: /workspace/dataset/test20_executable '<word>'      (exactly one argument)
It prints exactly 20 lines to stdout, one per API call, in this fixed order (1-indexed):
  1  pluralize(word)
  2  singularize(word)
  3  camelize(word)                       // default 2nd param
  4  camelize(word, false)
  5  underscore(word)
  6  classify(word)
  7  tableize(word)
  8  humanize(word)
  9  titleize(word)
  10 dasherize(word)
  11 parameterize(word)
  12 parameterize("A " + word + " Test")
  13 upcase(word)
  14 downcase(word)
  15 capitalize(word)
  16 decapitalize(word)
  17 truncate(word, 5)
  18 demodulize("Test::" + word)
  19 to_string(isPlural(word))    -> "0"/"1"
  20 to_string(isSingular(word))  -> "0"/"1"

With no argument it prints nothing. With an empty argument it ABORTS (std::out_of_range from
basic_string::substr inside demodulize) printing nothing to stdout.

TOOLING TIPS
- Extract one line:  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable 'word' | sed -n '5p'
- Show exact bytes:  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable 'word' | sed -n '5p' | od -c
- Loop:  for w in a b c; do printf '%s -> ' "$w"; /workspace/dataset/test20_executable "$w" | sed -n '5p'; done
- Use $'...' bash quoting for control bytes / high bytes, e.g. $'a\tb', $'\xc3\xa9'.
- 'file' is unavailable; 'strings', 'od', 'sed', 'nl' work.
- The binary is fast; run HUNDREDS of probes. Be exhaustive, not economical.

GROUND RULES
- Every claim in your output MUST be backed by an observed probe you actually ran.
- Assume C locale: toupper/tolower/isalnum/isspace behave as ASCII-only; bytes >= 0x80 are
  unchanged by case ops and are NOT alnum. VERIFY this rather than assuming.
- Note operations are byte-based (std::string), not char-based. Test multi-byte UTF-8.
- Report the algorithm as precise pseudocode that a Rust programmer can transcribe with zero guessing,
  operating on BYTES.


YOUR ASSIGNMENT (parameterize):
Characterize line 11 parameterize(word) and line 12 parameterize("A " + word + " Test").
Hypothesis: map each byte: isalnum -> tolower ; isspace -> '-' ; otherwise DROP.
Then trim leading and trailing '-' (but do NOT squeeze internal runs).
Evidence: "hello_world"->"helloworld", "a-b"->"ab", "Hello World"->"hello-world",
"  spaced  "->"spaced" while line 12 for that input is "a---spaced---test".
Verify precisely:
 - which whitespace bytes map to '-' (space, \t, \n, \v, \f, \r) - use $'...' quoting;
 - whether '-' and '_' in the input are dropped or become separators;
 - whether internal runs are squeezed (try "a  b", "a - b", "a__b");
 - exact trimming semantics (only '-'? also whitespace? leading only? how many?);
 - a word that is entirely non-alnum (e.g. "---", "...", "  ") -> what comes out (and cross-check
   with line 12 which embeds it);
 - UTF-8 handling byte by byte;
 - digits preserved; uppercase lowered.
Use line 12 to infer behavior for inputs whose line-11 result is empty. Run 80+ probes.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text: Model verified against 1000 randomized differential probes with zero mismatches. Reporting.

uncertainties: Byte 0x00 cannot be passed through argv, so its behavior is untestable from the CLI. By analogy with every other control byte (0x01-0x1F all dropped) it would almost certainly be dropped, but this is inference, not observation.

I cannot distinguish between an implementation that trims with a repeated pop/erase loop and one that uses find_first_not_of('-')/find_last_not_of('-') and substr — they are behaviorally identical for every input. The Rust sketch uses the position/rposition form, which matches all 1350 probes.

I cannot distinguish 'map then trim' from 'trim-then-map' variants that happen to coincide, but ' . a' -> 'a' and 'a . ' -> 'a' rule out any variant that trims the raw input's whitespace before mapping, which was the only plausible alternative.

parameterize on a truly empty string is not directly observable because the harness aborts in demodulize before printing. Line 12 for words that map to nothing ('.', '-', '_') is consistent with parameterize('') returning '' , so the empty-input path is inferred rather than directly observed.

The exhaustive byte sweep used the context 'a' + byte + 'b'. A hypothetical position-dependent or context-dependent rule (e.g. a byte behaving differently at index 0) is not fully excluded by that sweep alone, though the 1000 randomized differential probes with varied positions and lengths found zero disagreements, which makes any such rule very unlikely.

apis.name: parameterize
apis.pseudocode:
parameterize(input: bytes) -> bytes

STEP 1 - per-byte map (no lookahead, no state, purely positional):
  out = []
  for each byte b in input:
      if b in 0x30..=0x39 ('0'..'9'):   out.push(b)            # digits kept as-is
      elif b in 0x61..=0x7A ('a'..'z'): out.push(b)            # lowercase kept as-is
      elif b in 0x41..=0x5A ('A'..'Z'): out.push(b + 0x20)     # uppercase -> lowercase, ASCII only
      elif b == 0x20 (SPACE):           out.push(0x2D '-')     # ONLY the space byte becomes '-'
      else:                             DROP b (emit nothing)

  CORRECTION TO THE STATED HYPOTHESIS: it is NOT isspace().
  Only 0x20 maps to '-'. The other C-locale whitespace bytes 0x09 \t, 0x0A \n,
  0x0B \v, 0x0C \f, 0x0D \r are DROPPED exactly like punctuation.
  Verified by exhaustive sweep of every byte 0x01..0xFF.
  Also dropped: '-' (0x2D) and '_' (0x5F) in the INPUT, all ASCII punctuation,
  all control bytes, 0x7F, and every high byte 0x80..=0xFF (so UTF-8 multi-byte
  sequences vanish entirely, byte by byte - no case folding, no substitution).

STEP 2 - trim '-' from BOTH ends, unbounded, no squeezing:
  start = index of first byte in out that is != '-'   (out.find_first_not_of('-'))
  if no such byte exists:  return ""                  (out was empty or all '-')
  end   = index of last  byte in out that is != '-'   (out.find_last_not_of('-'))
  return out[start ..= end]

  Trimming removes ALL leading and ALL trailing '-' (verified with 10 leading /
  10 trailing spaces), NOT just one. Internal runs of '-' are NEVER squeezed:
  N consecutive spaces in the interior produce exactly N '-' (verified N=1..8).
  The trim operates on the MAPPED RESULT, not on the raw input: input
  ' . a' (space, dot, space, 'a') maps to '--a' and trims to 'a'; if the code had
  instead trimmed input whitespace first it would have produced '-a'.

Output is always pure ASCII [a-z0-9-], can never contain a newline, and can be empty.

LINE 12 is exactly parameterize("A " + word + " Test") - same function, no special
casing. It is an oracle when line 11 is empty: the surrounding "A " and " Test"
prevent the interior '-' from being trimmed, so the interior dash count is visible.
For a word that is k spaces and nothing else, line 12 = 'a' + (k+2) dashes + 'test'.

'-' (0x2D) and '_' (0x5F) present in the INPUT are dropped, not treated as separators: 'a-b' -> 'ab', 'a__b' -> 'ab', 'Hello-World' -> 'helloworld'.
Internal runs are NEVER squeezed: 'a  b' -> 'a--b', 'a        b' -> 'a' + 8 dashes + 'b'. Only the two ends are trimmed.
Trimming is unbounded on both ends: 10 leading spaces and 10 trailing spaces both collapse to nothing.
Trimming acts on the MAPPED output, not on input whitespace. ' . a' -> 'a' (mapped '--a'), not '-a'. Equivalent to find_first_not_of('-') / find_last_not_of('-') + substr.

An input that maps entirely to '-' or to nothing yields the empty string: '---', '...', '  ', ' ', '-', '_', '.', UTF-8 accents, CJK, 0x7F bytes all -> '' on line 11. Line 12 still reveals the interior dash count.

Digits 0-9 preserved verbatim; A-Z lowered by +0x20; a-z unchanged. Nothing else survives.
Output alphabet is strictly [a-z0-9-]; it can never contain whitespace, a newline, or a non-ASCII byte, and it never starts or ends with '-'.
